final_text:
Short answer: it’s almost entirely confounding and measurement choice.

What the NHANES meta-analyses actually show when set up appropriately
- When we use the diastolic mean (MDIASTOLIC) instead of the first reading and pool across cycles, dietary potassium and magnesium are associated with lower diastolic BP, in line with RCTs:
  - Potassium (DR1TPOTA) → MDIASTOLIC: β = −0.036 (SE 0.0087), p = 0.0042, 8 cycles
  - Magnesium (DR1TMAGN) → MDIASTOLIC: β = −0.038 (SE 0.0086), p = 0.0031, 8 cycles
- Sodium (DR1TSODI) → MDIASTOLIC does not yield a robust meta-analytic signal in our catalog (null in model 6).
- Using the first diastolic reading (BPXDI1), the EP-WAS atlas has no robust exposure hits (empty scan), which is consistent with much higher noise in a single reading.

Why you can get “all positive” slopes with dietary (DR1T*) variables
- Calorie confounding and collinearity with diet size:
  - Sodium, potassium, magnesium, and total calories move together very strongly in NHANES; pairwise r with energy (kcal) are high (e.g., kcal–sodium r ≈ 0.80; kcal–potassium r ≈ 0.73; kcal–magnesium r ≈ 0.73; sodium–potassium r ≈ 0.65). If you don’t energy-adjust, each nutrient partially proxies total intake/diet size.
- Body-size confounding (and model 6 omits BMI and calories):
  - Model 6 in the EP-WAS (age + age² + sex + ethnicity) does not adjust for calories or BMI. Sodium intake is positively related to BMI (β ≈ +0.093, p ≈ 4e−5), and BMI increases BP. Without appropriate energy/BMI adjustment, DR1T nutrients can all inherit a positive slope with BP via diet size/body size.
  - Potassium and magnesium also show strong ties to dietary patterns and albumin/inflammation markers, highlighting non-specific confounding in DR1T variables.
- Measurement choice and noise:
  - A single diastolic reading is noisy; within-visit SD for BP is ~3 mmHg. Using BPXDI1 instead of the averaged measure (MDIASTOLIC) inflates random error and can yield unstable or misleading associations.
- Reverse causality and treatment muddle sodium:
  - Diagnosed hypertensives often restrict sodium and use antihypertensives, which can attenuate or flip cross-sectional sodium–BP associations. Sensitivity analyses that exclude/adjust for diagnosed disease and meds are needed.

Triangulation with RCTs
- RCT meta-analyses show the expected BP-lowering effects:
  - Sodium reduction: ΔDBP ≈ −2.8 mmHg (He 2013; BMJ)
  - Potassium supplementation: ΔDBP ≈ −3.0 mmHg in hypertensives (Filippini 2020; JAHA)
  - Magnesium supplementation: ΔDBP ≈ −2.1 mmHg (AHA 2025; Hypertension)
- The NHANES pooled observational signals for K and Mg (using MDIASTOLIC) agree in direction with these RCTs.

How to fix analyses so NHANES agrees with trials
- Use the averaged diastolic BP (MDIASTOLIC), not BPXDI1.
- Energy-adjust nutrient intakes (nutrient density or residual method) and include total kcal in the model.
- Adjust for BMI (and ideally waist), smoking, and meds; run sensitivity analyses excluding diagnosed hypertension.
- Prefer urinary biomarkers (24-h sodium/potassium or Na/K ratio) over single-day dietary recall when possible.
- Model usual intake if you have both Day 1 and Day 2 recalls.

Bottom line
The “all positive” pattern with DR1T sodium/potassium/magnesium and diastolic BP comes from using single-day dietary recalls that are tightly collinear with calories and body size, plus noisy single BP readings and lack of energy/BMI adjustment. When you switch to the averaged BP outcome and handle energy/BMI properly, NHANES aligns with RCT evidence (potassium/magnesium lower DBP; sodium reduction lowers DBP). If you share your model/code, I can validate it for these issues and re-run with the recommended adjustments.
